operations.evidence: One safety-management model uses Plan, Do, Check and Act to set policy, implement controls, measure performance and learn.
The model is optional and must be adapted to the building.
A safety management system does not have to be accredited to an external standard; it must work effectively for the organisation and building.
Absence of accreditation is not evidence of poor performance, and accreditation is not proof of legal compliance.
The system should be based on the building risk assessment and proportionate to building complexity, controls, portfolio, organisation, contractors and resident profile.
A portfolio-wide template must not replace building-specific analysis.
Safety-management documents should be concise and easily understood.
Brevity must not omit material risk, control or accountability information.
An effective system regularly reviews and updates controls, policies and procedures and identifies areas for improvement.
An improvement plan is not evidence that improvements have been delivered.
Improvement plans should state objectives, reasons, timescales, resources and named leaders, with senior managers measuring progress.
Named ownership does not prove completion or effectiveness.
Senior leadership should support the system, influence safety culture and provide resources.
Leadership statements alone are not evidence that resources are sufficient.
Specific safety roles should be defined and supported by competence, training, authority and budgets.
A job title does not establish competence or authority.
Organisations should have systems to verify contractor competence, including appropriate evidence and checks.
Certification alone does not prove suitability for every task or building.
Systems should schedule, undertake and record maintenance and inspection work and retain evidence of completion and remediation.
A scheduled task is not evidence it was completed correctly or on time.
Reports and certificates should be reviewed and identified actions tracked to completion.
Receipt of a certificate does not prove that all actions were closed.
Change management should cover changes to the building, residents, management systems and changes made by others that affect safety.
A change category does not establish its actual impact without assessment.
Effective monitoring uses leading indicators such as timely maintenance and fire-door inspections and lagging indicators such as incidents and breakdowns.
Indicators must not be averaged in a way that hides individual-building performance.
The system should be reviewed after incidents, performance dips, feedback, complaints, changes to buildings or dutyholders, legal updates and scheduled reviews.
A review trigger does not itself demonstrate a breach or failure.
The strategy explains how residents and residential-unit owners are involved in and informed about building safety decisions.
Engagement is not a substitute for technical safety assessment.
The PAP must prepare, follow, review and revise the strategy, keep review records, provide it to APs and consult when necessary.
Preparation of a strategy does not prove that engagement duties are being performed effectively.
Accountable persons must provide the latest strategy to residents in their parts and work with other accountable persons to update it.
Distribution cannot be assumed without delivery evidence.
The PAP should prepare the strategy as soon as possible when the building becomes occupied or they become the PAP.
The trigger date must be determined from building-specific occupancy and appointment evidence.
The PAP must submit the strategy when BSR directs it to apply for a building assessment certificate.
Submission does not mean BSR has approved every part of the strategy.
A strategy should be specific to the building and reflect residents' needs and preferences.
A generic portfolio template is not sufficient evidence of building-specific engagement.
The strategy should describe which decisions residents will be asked about and what information they will receive, including communication method and work timing.
Information provision does not transfer statutory decision responsibility to residents.
For work lasting more than one day that blocks part of the building or disrupts residents, the PAP must ask about timing and minimising disruption.
Consultation does not allow necessary safety work to be omitted.
Residents do not need to be consulted before immediate emergency repairs needed to protect health, safety or welfare.
The exception applies to urgent protective repairs and should not be used for ordinary planned work.
Engagement can use post, websites, email, social media, apps, meetings or visits.
Offering a channel does not prove it is accessible or effective for all residents.
The strategy should consider language and alternative formats such as large text, easy read, braille or audio.
A listed format must not be treated as delivered unless resident needs and actual provision are verified.
The strategy should explain how opinions are collected, reviewed and acted on, how feedback is provided, timescales and GDPR-compliant storage.
Collection of opinions does not require adoption of every suggestion.
Participation can be reviewed using response counts, surveys, focus groups, meetings and visits, with results recorded.
Response volume alone does not measure the quality or representativeness of engagement.
Consultation on the first strategy and changes must include residents and APs and last at least three weeks.
A three-week period does not by itself prove meaningful participation.
The PAP must review the strategy at least every two years, after mandatory occurrence reports and after significant material alterations, and record every review.
A review record is not evidence that identified improvements were implemented.
